newsitem.title: UK: Europe well placed to supply US gasoline market.
newsitem.headline: Europe well placed to supply US gasoline market.

text.p: Western Europe, which accounts for 25 percent of U.S. gasoline imports, is well supplied for the thirsty driving season even though inventories have dried up a bit on both sides of the Atlantic, analysts and traders said.

Oil prices are starting to react to the approach of the spring and summer gasoline markets just as they focused on the tight heating oil inventories ahead of last winter, when crude and gas oil rocketed up to six-year highs.

Although most analysts ruled out a supply crunch based only on European fundamentals, some thought a protracted winter or a sudden surge in U.S. demand for gasoline could erode some of the surplus and lead to price spikes.

Excess refinery capacity and sluggish demand in Europe has reduced the chance of a supply crunch in the gasoline market and the analysts said any strength would have to come from the U.S. market. The scenario of tight distillate stocks which dominated the fourth quarter of 1996 was not likely to be repeated, they added.
"I think the underlying situation is still pretty weak," said Colin Birch, a consultant at Purvin and Gertz in London. "Ten percent of the production is excess to local demand."
Although prices for premium unleaded gasoline have sunk to $216 a tonne in Rotterdam from a four-year high of $240 last October, they are still $50 a tonne, or 24 percent, stronger than a year ago.
"There is definitely no tightness in the physical market," said one trader. "The first-half February is dried up but from then on there is plenty (of supply)...I'm bearish."
The value of gasoline compared to Brent crude also hints at an underlying weakness in the market.
Gasoline swaps for the second quarter are some $5.10 a barrel above Brent, compared to an average of more than $6 a barrel for the same period in 1996.
European gasoline supplies, excluding Sweden, fell to 155.59 million barrels at the end of December, down 5.89 million or 3.6 percent from a year, according to recent Euroilstock data.

And in January, as much as two million tonnes was sucked out of Northwest Europe and the Mediterranean after the arbitrage door to the U.S. swung open, traders said. Some interest started to creep up for February as well.
Birch said demand was showing signs of perking up after several years of flat or negative growth.
But exports will likely hold near year-ago levels while several refinery closures in Europe will have only a marginal effect on gasoline output, he said.

European countries, led by Britain, Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands, exported 25.5 million barrels of finished motor gasoline to the U.S. in the first 10 months of 1996, up from 19.5 million for all of 1995, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
"You look to the U.S. for potential upside in prices this time of year, not to Europe," an analyst said.

Indeed, some analysts said if U.S. prices rallied and draw more barrels out of Europe, or another blast of cold weather hit Europe or the U.S., then gasoline inventories could dry up and support prices.
"I think there is quite a real risk that gasoline inventories when the driving season starts could be very low," said one commission house analyst here.
"Gasoline could be leading the charge if products prices continue to underpin crude," he said.
U.S. gasoline inventories rose last week by 1.8 million barrels to 201.3 million, but are still at an 11.0 million deficit to their year-ago level.
